brief_summary: ProsBiT is a prospective multicenter observational cohort study that collects standardized data on men undergoing prostate biopsy for suspected prostate cancer at 24 urology centers in Turkey. Clinical, laboratory, imaging, procedural, pathology, complication, and patient-reported pain data are recorded in a common electronic case report form (REDCap). The study aims to compare transperineal and transrectal biopsy in terms of cancer detection, complications, and patient comfort; to evaluate how MRI findings (PI-RADS) and PSA density predict clinically significant prostate cancer, including external validation of published risk-adapted biopsy strategies; to describe variation in biopsy practice between centers; to assess bleeding risk in men using antithrombotic drugs; to examine the agreement between MRI lesion location and biopsy-positive zones; and to describe the learning curve of transperineal biopsy. No intervention is assigned by the study; all diagnostic and treatment decisions are made by the treating physicians according to routine practice.
primary_outcomes: Detection rate of clinically significant prostate cancer
title: ProsBiT: Turkish Prostate Biopsy Study

brief_summary: Levetiracetam may be removed during continuous renal replacement therapy (CRRT), potentially affecting drug concentrations and seizure control. The optimal dosing regimen for critically ill patients receiving CRRT remains unclear. This observational study will investigate the pharmacokinetics of levetiracetam in critically ill adult patients receiving CRRT. Blood, CRRT effluent, and urine samples will be collected throughout one dosing interval to measure levetiracetam concentrations. The data will be used to develop a population pharmacokinetic model and perform pharmacokinetic/pharmacodynamic modeling and Monte Carlo simulations to evaluate dosing regimens and estimate the probability of achieving predefined drug concentration or exposure targets. The findings may help identify an appropriate levetiracetam dosing regimen for critically ill patients receiving CRRT.
primary_outcomes: Probability of target attainment for simulated levetiracetam dosing regimens
title: Pharmacokinetics and Optimal Dosing of Levetiracetam in Critically Ill Patients Undergoing Continuous Renal Replacement Therapy

brief_summary: Purple Town is a media literacy-based prevention and harm reduction program that uses a mobile game, with or without accompanying facilitated workshops, to raise young people's awareness of the risks associated with alcohol and cannabis use. The program aims to develop critical thinking about marketing messages and encourage the adoption of protective behavioral strategies. This study evaluated the effectiveness of the program through a cluster randomized controlled trial (CRCT) among youth.
primary_outcomes: Skepticism Toward Marketing Scale score

Awareness of Marketing Influence Strategies Questionnaire score
Protective Behavioral Intentions Questionnaire score
Alcohol and Cannabis Lifetime Use Questionnaire Status

brief_summary:
The goal of this randomized controlled trial is to compare the efficacy of topical luliconazole with topical bifonazole in adults aged 18-60 years with dermatophytosis. All participants will receive oral itraconazole, while either topical luliconazole or topical bifonazole will be added according to their assigned treatment group. The main questions it aims to answer are:

* Does topical luliconazole result in greater improvement in clinical severity, as measured by the DeASI score, compared with topical bifonazole?
* Does topical luliconazole result in better mycological clearance on 10% KOH microscopy and lower relapse compared with topical bifonazole? Researchers will compare topical luliconazole with topical bifonazole, with oral itraconazole given to both groups, to assess differences in clinical improvement, mycological cure, and relapse.

Participants will:

* Receive oral itraconazole 100 mg once daily together with either topical luliconazole 1% or topical bifonazole 1% once daily for 28 days.
* Attend follow-up visits at weeks 2, 4, and 6 for clinical assessment, DeASI scoring, and 10% KOH microscopy.
primary_outcomes: Mean reduction in DeASI score from baseline to Week 4
title: Comparative Efficacy of Luliconazole and Bifonazole Combined With Itraconazole in Dermatophytosis

brief_summary:
LEANDIP is a multicentric, prospective comparative longitudinal phenotyping study designed to characterize lean diabetes (BMI \<19 kg/m²) in Asian Indians and determine whether it represents a distinct metabolic and biological phenotype.

Study population: 151 participants - Lean diabetes (n=75), healthy lean controls (n=38), and non-lean/classical T2D (n=38).

Baseline phenotyping: Clinical and anthropometric assessment, biochemical investigations, insulin/C-peptide assessment with MMTT, body composition by DEXA, and assessment of diabetes-related complications where applicable.

Advanced phenotyping: MRI-PDFF for pancreatic, hepatic and abdominal fat; genomic analysis in lean diabetes and healthy lean controls; and metabolomics in predefined subsets.

Comparative objective: To identify clinical, metabolic, body-composition, imaging, genomic and metabolomic characteristics specific to lean diabetes compared with healthy leanness and classical T2D.

Longitudinal component: Lean diabetes participants will be followed at 6 and 12 months to assess glycaemic progression, complications, treatment requirements and changes in phenotype.

Overall aim: To improve understanding of the biological basis, pancreatic dysfunction, ectopic fat phenotype and clinical progression of lean diabetes in Asian Indians, potentially enabling better identification and management of this under-recognized phenotype.
interventions: The study does not involve any therapeutic or lifestyle intervention. Participants will undergo clinical evaluation, biochemical testing, genomic and metabolomic analysis, BCA, pancreatic imaging.
primary_outcomes: Primary Outcome: Genomic and Metabolomic Characterization of Lean Diabetes
title: LEANDIP: Lean Diabetes in Asian Indians

brief_summary:
Ulcerative colitis (UC) is a long-term inflammatory bowel condition. Many patients are treated with intravenous biologic drugs such as infliximab or vedolizumab. Measuring the level of these drugs in the blood helps doctors adjust treatment, but results can take one to two weeks to come back.

Volatile organic compounds (VOCs) are gases released from stool and urine that reflect activity in the gut, including gut bacteria and inflammation. They can be measured quickly and without needles.

This study will find out whether VOCs in stool and urine can tell apart patients with adequate drug levels from those with low drug levels. It will also look at whether VOCs can identify patients whose UC is in remission versus those whose disease is flaring, and how VOCs relate to blood inflammation markers, gut bacteria and DNA methylation (chemical tags on genes).

Adults with UC already receiving maintenance intravenous infliximab or vedolizumab at University Hospitals Coventry and Warwickshire will be invited to take part. Participants will provide stool, urine and blood samples at four of their routine infusion appointments. No extra visits are needed and treatment is not changed by the study.
lead_sponsor: University Hospitals Coventry and Warwickshire NHS Trust
primary_outcomes: Faecal VOC discrimination of therapeutic versus sub-therapeutic biologic trough concentration
title: Non-Invasive Biomarker Monitoring in UC on Biologics

brief_summary:
The goal of this observational study is to learn if providing meal kits during pregnancy is helpful for people experiencing food insecurity. The study will also learn about participants' experiences with receiving meal kits during pregnancy and after giving birth. The main questions it aims to answer are:

* Does receiving meal kits affect pregnancy and health outcomes?
* How do participants experience and use the meal kits?
* What benefits or challenges do participants report when receiving the meal kits?

Participants who screen positive for food insecurity during routine prenatal care will be offered weekly meal kits through Meals on Wheels Rhode Island (MoWRI). Participants who accept the meal program will receive meal kits throughout pregnancy and through two weeks after giving birth. Participants who do not enroll in the meal program will continue to receive their usual prenatal care and referrals to food and nutrition resources.

Participants will:

* Complete surveys about their health, food access, and experiences with the meal program.
* Continue their regular prenatal care.
* Some participants will be invited to complete an interview about their experiences.
lead_sponsor: Women and Infants Hospital of Rhode Island
primary_outcomes: Qualitative perceptions of nutritional support and dietary quality among program participants
Proportion of participants experiencing any maternal medical complication
title: Addressing Food Insecurity in Pregnancy

brief_summary:
This study evaluated the effects of non-surgical periodontal therapy on periodontal health and inflammatory markers in patients with periodontitis, with and without type 2 diabetes mellitus.

Participants were divided into three groups according to their diabetes status and glycemic control: patients without diabetes, patients with well-controlled type 2 diabetes, and patients with poorly controlled type 2 diabetes.

Periodontal clinical measurements and gingival crevicular fluid and blood samples were collected at baseline. Participants subsequently received non-surgical periodontal therapy. Clinical measurements and biological samples were collected again three months after treatment.

The study assessed changes in periodontal clinical parameters and inflammatory biomarkers, including interleukin-4 (IL-4) and interleukin-17 (IL-17), to investigate whether responses to periodontal treatment differed according to diabetes status and glycemic control.
primary_outcomes: Change in Gingival Crevicular Fluid and Serum IL-4 Levels
title: IL-4 and IL-17 Responses to Periodontal Therapy in Patients With Type 2 Diabetes

brief_summary: Prostate cancer is a major malignancy in men, and prostate biopsy determines both cancer detection and risk stratification. Biopsy strategies vary substantially across centers in approach (transperineal vs. transrectal), use of multiparametric MRI (mpMRI), targeted versus systematic sampling, and the spatial distribution of cores; however, most prior databases record only the total number of cores and cannot reconstruct the spatial location of individual cores. This national multicenter, retrospective, non-interventional observational cohort study, led by Guangxi Medical University and involving more than 20 hospitals across more than 10 provinces in China, will establish a layered database linking patients, MRI lesions, biopsy events, actual needle passes/specimen jars/cores, and radical prostatectomy pathology, and will convert historical needle-placement strategies into unified, auditable spatial variables. The study aims to compare the detection rate and per-core detection efficiency of ISUP Grade Group (GG) \>=2 prostate cancer across different spatial needle-placement strategies, to estimate the absolute missed-cancer cost and core-saving benefit of candidate reduced templates through within-patient reconstruction, and to evaluate the concordance, upgrading, and downgrading between biopsy and radical prostatectomy GG. The study adds no tests, biopsies, treatment, or follow-up, and the main risks are privacy breach and data misuse. Target enrollment is at least 30,000 cases.
primary_outcomes: Grade Group >=2 Prostate Cancer Detection Rate
Per-Needle-Pass Grade Group >=2 Detection Efficiency
Absolute Grade Group >=2 Omission Rate of Candidate Reduced Templates
Biopsy-Radical Prostatectomy Grade Group Concordance
title: Spatial Needle Placement Strategies and Pathological Concordance in Prostate Biopsy: A National Multicenter Retrospective Cohort Study

brief_summary:
The goal of this clinical trial is to further characterize the safety profile of saypha® ChIQ™ for midface augmentation in adults with Fitzpatrick Skin Types V and VI who have moderate to severe midface volume deficit.

The main questions it aims to answer are whether treatment with saypha® ChIQ™ has an acceptable safety profile, as assessed by the incidence and nature of treatment-emergent adverse events, including adverse device effects, injection site reactions, symptoms of interest, and ocular safety findings through 24 weeks after the last injection, and whether treatment improves midface volume deficit and subject-reported aesthetic outcomes in this study population.

Participants will receive treatment with saypha® ChIQ™ at baseline, with an optional touch-up treatment approximately 2 weeks later if clinically indicated, attend scheduled follow-up visits for safety and effectiveness assessments for up to 24 weeks after the last injection; and complete subject-reported outcome assessments and safety diaries as specified in the protocol.
conditions: Moderate to Severe Midface Volume Deficit
interventions: Crosslinked hyaluronic acid dermal filler with lidocaine
primary_outcomes: Incidence of treatment-emergent adverse events (TEAEs)
title: Post-Approval Study of Saypha® ChIQ™ for Midface Augmentation in Subjects With Fitzpatrick Skin Types V and VI

brief_summary: This study evaluates the effect of a nursing-led Enhanced Recovery After Surgery (ERAS) protocol on recovery among adults undergoing emergency laparotomy. A total of 120 eligible patients aged 18-65 years were randomly assigned to either a study group receiving the nursing-led ERAS protocol in addition to routine postoperative care or a control group receiving routine postoperative care alone. The protocol includes respiratory care, pain and nausea management, early mobilization, nutritional support, prevention of postoperative complications, catheter and drain management, psychosocial support, and patient education and discharge planning. Postoperative pain, recovery milestones, complications, hospital readmission, length of hospital stay, and satisfaction with nursing care are assessed.
interventions: Nursing-Led Enhanced Recovery After Surgery (ERAS) Protocol
primary_outcomes: Postoperative Pain Intensity
Time to First Passage of Flatus
Time to First Bowel Movement
Length of Hospital Stay
title: Nursing-Led ERAS Protocol for Improving Recovery After Emergency Laparotomy

brief_summary:
The goal of this clinical trial is to compare the safety of dipyrone and paracetamol when used for pain relief after dental extractions in adults. The study will focus on changes in blood cell counts and will also evaluate liver and kidney function and possible side effects. The main questions it aims to answer are:

* Do dipyrone and paracetamol have different effects on blood cell counts after dental extractions?
* Do participants exhibit hepatic and renal alterations?
* What side effects do participants experience when taking these medications?

brief_summary:
The REACT study is for people with a rare type of cancer called T-cell lymphoma. T-cell lymphoma affects cells that are part of the body's immune system.

Most lymphomas develop from B cells. Lymphomas that develop from T cells are much rarer. There are several different types of T-cell lymphoma, and many of them grow quickly. Without treatment, people with aggressive T-cell lymphoma may die within weeks or months. Even when the first treatment is successful, only about 25 to 40 out of 100 patients are still alive without the lymphoma returning two years after diagnosis.

Treatment usually involves several courses of chemotherapy, given every two or three weeks. In most patients, the lymphoma becomes smaller during treatment. However, in about one in three patients, the lymphoma starts to grow again while they are still receiving treatment. In other patients, the lymphoma becomes smaller but does not disappear completely. In these cases, it often returns within weeks or months after treatment has finished.

Stem cell transplantation

If the lymphoma gets worse during treatment or returns soon afterwards, a blood stem cell transplant may offer the best chance of a cure. This treatment replaces the patient's immune system with a new immune system from a healthy donor, which can recognize and eliminate the lymphoma cells.

For a stem cell transplant, doctors need to find a healthy donor whose tissue characteristics are a good match for the patient. These characteristics can be checked with a blood test. Sometimes a suitable donor can be found within the patient's family. More often, doctors search for an unrelated volunteer donor whose information is stored in a donor database.

A stem cell transplant has a better chance of being successful if the lymphoma can first be brought under control with additional chemotherapy.

In everyday clinical practice, however, stem cell transplantation is often delayed or cannot be reached. For example, it may take time to find a suitable donor, or treatment given after the lymphoma has returned may fail. Additional treatment may also make patients weaker and less able to undergo a stem cell transplant.

For these reasons, it is important to identify patients whose lymphoma is not responding well to their first treatment as early as possible. Patients whose lymphoma returns only several years after their first treatment generally have a better outlook.

What is different in the REACT study?

The REACT study uses two main approaches. First, the search for a suitable stem cell donor starts soon after diagnosis for all patients taking part in the study. This means that a donor may already be available if a stem cell transplant becomes necessary.

Second, patients have a special scan after only two courses of chemotherapy. This scan combines computed tomography (CT) with positron emission tomography (PET) and is called a PET/CT scan. The scan shows how well the lymphoma is responding to treatment. It can help doctors identify patients who have a high risk of the lymphoma returning.

The researchers hope that combining an early donor search with early PET/CT scans will improve the treatment of T-cell lymphoma. If the scan suggests that the lymphoma is likely to return, doctors can consider a stem cell transplant earlier, while the patient is still in a good enough condition to receive it.

Who can take part?

Patients may be able to take part in the REACT study if their doctors believe that a blood stem cell transplant from a family member or an unrelated donor would be suitable for them. They must also have one of the following types of T-cell lymphoma:

* Peripheral T-cell lymphoma, not otherwise specified (PTCL-NOS)
* Nodal T-follicular helper cell lymphoma (nTFHL), including angioimmunoblastic, follicular, and NOS subtypes
* ALK-negative anaplastic large cell lymphoma (ALK-negative ALCL) All patients receive the standard chemotherapy that their doctors consider most suitable. This may follow the CHOP, CHOEP, or BV-CHP treatment protocol.

If the early PET/CT scan suggests a high risk that the lymphoma will return, or if the lymphoma actually returns, doctors will aim to carry out a stem cell transplant as soon as possible. If standard chemotherapy works well and there are no signs that the lymphoma is likely to return, a stem cell transplant is not performed.

The overall aim of the REACT study is to identify patients at high risk of relapse earlier and, when needed, make stem cell transplantation possible at an earlier and potentially more effective stage of treatment.

The aim of this trial is to investigate the effect of the activation of C-tactile afferents (CT) on relapse predicting biomarkers and subjective alcohol craving in alcohol use disorder (AUD) patients.

To test this in a laboratory environment, we will investigate the acute and chronic effect of mechanic CT activation vs. non-CT-activating control condition during exposure to validated craving-inducing visual stimuli in patients with AUD.We will assess several physiological measures that have been previously shown to indicate craving and predict relapse in patients with substance use disorder. These measures include pupillary reactivity, electroencephalography (EEG), salivary cortisol level and heart rate variability (HRV). These measures, together with the ratings of subjective craving, will be the primary endpoints of the investigation.

Primary objective is to test the hypothesis that CT activation may have therapeutic potential in treatment of AUD. Secondary objective is to investigate the safety and tolerability of mechanic optimal CT activation and its feasibility on modulation of certain biomarkers in AUD population.

40 early abstinent (≥ 2 weeks) female and male individuals of 18 to 60 years of age who meet the Diagnostic and Statistical Manual of Mental Disorders, 5th Edition (DSM-5) criteria for mild to moderate AUD and who commonly engage in heavy alcohol consumption. However, the participants should precede two weeks of abstinence.

The study will include two experiments (Experiment 1. and Experiment 2.) that are conducted during two separate study visits with maximum seven days in between the visits.

Experiment 1. - Stress-related biomarkers in cue-, stress- and neutral stimuli exposure.

Experiment 1 aims to assess HPA-axis and autonomic nervoussystem reactivity before, during and after exposure to alcohol-, stress-, and neutral visual stimuli while either CT-optimal or non-CT-optimal robotic skin stimulation is provided. The primary biomarkers that will be monitored during the experiment are blood volume pulse (BVP), from which heart rate variability (HRV) will be derived from, and salivary cortisol level. In addition, self-reposted alcohol craving will be measuren with visual analog scale.

Five salivary cortisol samples will be collected at time points -20, -5, 0, +10 and +25. HRV will be derived from BVP and analysed with Kubios HRV Premium software.

All three visual stimuli conditions (neutral, alcohol and stress) will be given during the first study visit.

Experiment 2 - Cue-reactivity task test

In the cue-reactivity task pupillary reactivity, event related potentials (EVP's) of EEG will be measured during alcohol-related and neutral visual stimuli while the CT-optimal or non-CT-optimal skin stimulation is provided. Subjective craving will be self-reported by rating it on a 5-point VAS after each alcohol-related image.

The experiment will take place in an electrically shielded room provided by Aalto Behavioral Laboratory. The pupillary reactivity tracking and the EEG measuring systems will be connected to the PC providing the visual stimuli and the following tasks.

Two types of stimuli - 48 alcohol-related and 48 neutral images - will be presented so that each alcohol related image will be followed by a neutral image. The images will be centered on a white background and the colour, size and brightness of the alcohol and neutral stimuli will be matched. ). After each neutral image, the subject will be presented a question about the predominant colour in the image, which they will answer with the response pad. Once the subject has responded, the next stimulus image will be presented. The trial and the EEG and pupillometry recordings will finnish when the subject has responded to all images. In the end of the laboratory session, the subject will go through a relapse prevention session with an addiction medicine specialist to ensure that the distress caused by the experiments will not trigger a relapse outside of the laboratory.

Relapse prevention sessions

In both experiments the subjects will go through a relapse prevention session with an experienced addiction medicine specialist. The relapse prevention session will take place at the end of each laboratory session, after the exposure to the stimuli. The session consists of short motivational enhancement counselling designed to prevent relapsing.

Follow-up

The experiments will be followed by a two-week period during which the participant will report subjective craving, alcohol consumption and possible adverse events by filling an online diary (Appendix 6). If the participant does not have access to the internet, the diary may be filled manually.

Pancreatic mucinous cystic neoplasms (MCNs), serous cystic neoplasms (SCNs), and pancreatic pseudocysts (PPCs) often exhibit overlapping imaging features on endoscopic ultrasound (EUS). However, these conditions require different clinical management strategies. Accurate differentiation is therefore important for appropriate treatment planning.

This study aims to develop and validate an artificial intelligence (AI) model that integrates EUS images and clinical features to differentiate MCNs, SCNs, and PPCs. The study is designed as an ambispective observational diagnostic study consisting of retrospective model development, prospective temporal validation, and a reader study involving EUS physicians.

Approximately 400 adult patients with confirmed MCN, SCN, or PPC will be included. Retrospective clinical data and EUS images will be used for model development and internal validation. After model development is completed, newly diagnosed patients will be prospectively enrolled to independently evaluate the diagnostic performance of the model.

The primary outcome is the patient-level macro-averaged area under the receiver operating characteristic curve (macro-AUROC) for three-class classification in the prospective validation cohort. Secondary outcomes include diagnostic accuracy, sensitivity, specificity, calibration, clinical net benefit, and the performance of EUS physicians with and without AI assistance.

This study is expected to provide evidence for the potential clinical value of AI-assisted differentiation of pancreatic cystic lesions. No additional invasive procedures or study-specific treatments will be performed.

Although the eccentric exercise group achieved significantly greater strength gains and greater flexibility improvements over time compared to the neurodynamic sliding group, the overall between-group differences in flexibility across time points were not statistically significant and were confounded by baseline imbalances. Consequently, while both approaches are effective for this population, eccentric exercise demonstrated greater overall benefits, though the between-group flexibility advantages warrant cautious interpretation.

Chronic pain is common among people living with Alzheimer's disease and related dementias (ADRD) and can negatively affect daily functioning and quality of life. Music listening may help manage pain, but researchers do not fully understand how music influences brain activity and the body's physiological responses in people with dementia.

This exploratory pilot study will examine whether a standardized music listening intervention can be delivered successfully at home with caregiver assistance. It will also investigate how music listening affects brain activity, heart rate variability, and participant-reported pain, including whether responses differ between morning and afternoon sessions.

The study will enroll 20 community-dwelling adults aged 55 years or older with early-stage ADRD and chronic pain, each supported by an eligible adult caregiver. Using a randomized, counterbalanced, within-subject crossover design, each adult with ADRD will complete eight home-based listening sessions across four conditions: morning MUSIC CARE®, afternoon MUSIC CARE®, morning audiobook control, and afternoon audiobook control. Each condition will be repeated twice over approximately two weeks.

During each session, brain activity will be measured using electroencephalography (EEG), and heart rate variability (HRV) will be recorded using wearable sensors. Participants will report their pain intensity immediately before and after listening.

The primary outcomes will assess recruitment, retention, intervention adherence, acceptability, and the feasibility of obtaining usable EEG and HRV recordings at home. Secondary exploratory outcomes will examine pain intensity, pain interference, frontal alpha asymmetry, frontal midline theta power, and high-frequency HRV.

Findings will help researchers understand the feasibility and potential mechanisms of music-based pain modulation in ADRD and inform future clinical trials of home-based music interventions.

brief_summary:
The second stage of labor is a crucial phase during which the fetus progresses through the birth canal, a process significantly influenced by maternal positions. While adopting specific birthing positions during the second stage offers potential benefits for maternal and neonatal health, inappropriate positions can lead to negative short- and long-term consequences. These include severe perineal lacerations, postpartum hemorrhage, an increased risk of neonatal complications, and postpartum urinary incontinence.

Birthing positions are considered non-medical interventions because they alter physiological and anatomical adaptations during labor. These adaptations, related to pelvic dimensions, intrauterine pressure, and the progression of the fetal head through the birth canal, directly influence maternal and fetal outcomes. Studies have reported that horizontal positioning during labor increases the likelihood of cesarean delivery, assisted vaginal delivery, episiotomy, and abnormal fetal heart rates.

Conversely, upright positions offer several advantages during labor. They facilitate fetal descent by utilizing gravity, strengthen uterine contractions, reduce the risk of aortocaval compression, increase pelvic dimensions, and help maintain fetal flexion in the narrowest parts of the birth canal. In the squatting position, maternal hip flexion significantly alters the pelvic axis angles through which the fetal head progresses, facilitating spontaneous vaginal delivery. Furthermore, uterine contractions are stronger and more effective in achieving effacement and dilation in the squatting position, thereby significantly contributing to the progression of labor.

The World Health Organization (2018) Intrapartum Care Management Guidelines recommend supporting upright positions in the second stage of labor for a more positive birth experience. However, data remains limited regarding the optimal upright position for women during this stage. Accordingly, this randomized controlled experimental study was designed to examine the effects of the squatting position during the second stage of labor on obstetric, maternal, and neonatal outcomes in nulliparous women with low-risk pregnancies planning a vaginal delivery.
primary_outcomes: Duration of the second stage of labor
Need for operative or obstetric interventions during delivery
title: Effect of Squatting Position in the Second Stage of Labor on Birth Outcomes

This prospective cohort study will follow 78 postmenopausal women with obesity who are eligible for bariatric surgery at Cairo University hospitals: 39 women who undergo bariatric surgery (sleeve gastrectomy, Roux-en-Y gastric bypass or one-anastomosis gastric bypass) as part of their routine care, and 39 matched women who choose non-surgical medical and lifestyle management. The study will compare these changes between the two groups and examine whether changes in estradiol are associated with changes in endometrial thickness and with weight loss.

brief_summary:
Ex-vivo split liver transplantation (SLT) has been developed to increase organ availability and offer a rapid access to transplantation for pediatric recipients. Given the fact that in-situ liver graft splitting is both technically and logistically very challenging, ex-vivo liver graft splitting is the most frequently performed procedure in SLT in France. Due to technical aspects inherent to the ex-vivo split, these partial grafts have prolonged static cold storage time, which negatively impacts graft survival despite the use of optimal donors. Hypothermic Oxygenated Perfusion (HOPE) of whole liver grafts prior to transplantation has been shown to optimize preservation by reducing static cold storage and consequently mitigating ischemia-reperfusion injury with a positive impact on post-LT outcomes. HOPE may thereby also benefit partial liver grafts from ex-vivo splits and improve outcomes in both pediatric and adult recipients.

Several trials assessing various modalities of liver machine perfusion have been conducted, but none have included partial grafts. Moreover, although the feasibility and safety of liver graft splitting during HOPE have been demonstrated in recent publications and by our group, robust data on its impact on split liver transplantation (SLT) outcomes are still lacking.

AVS is used to determine if one or both adrenal glands are overproducing a hormone called aldosterone, which causes high blood pressure.

The two techniques compared were "simultaneous" AVS (taking blood samples from both adrenal veins at the same time) and "sequential" AVS (taking blood samples from one adrenal vein and then the other). The goal was to evaluate both techniques for identifying the source of the hormone problem and to compare their safety and efficiency.

The study retrospectively reviewed the medical records of 238 patients who underwent AVS without using a stimulating drug (ACTH). The study assessed catheter placement success, diagnostic concordance between the two methods, fluoroscopy time, radiation dose, and procedure-related complications.

brief_summary:
There is currently no consensus recommendation regarding the routine use of surveillance kidney allograft biopsies during the first year after transplantation. As a result, the decision to perform surveillance biopsies remains center-dependent, and their long-term clinical benefit has not been conclusively demonstrated.

Although surveillance biopsy is considered the gold standard for detecting subclinical rejection, it is an invasive and costly procedure that carries a risk of complications. Furthermore, approximately 30-35% of surveillance biopsies reveal normal or near-normal histology, highlighting the need for strategies that can safely reduce unnecessary biopsies and improve patient comfort while optimizing healthcare resource utilization.

At Nantes University Hospital, three blood and urinary biomarkers predictive of the absence of rejection are routinely used to assess the relevance of performing a surveillance biopsy. The objective of this observational study is to evaluate patients' perceived stress related to the 1-year surveillance biopsy according to whether the procedure is maintained or canceled based on the results of these non-invasive biomarkers used in standard clinical practice.

brief_summary:
Primary Objective: The primary objective of the study is to characterize subjects affected by adrenal disease by collecting medical history data at diagnosis, clinical, bio-humoral, and radiological data, as well as information regarding the therapeutic approach, in terms of both potential surgical interventions and/or pharmacological therapies and hormone replacement therapies.

Secondary Objective: The secondary objective is to integrate these data with current knowledge in order to improve the clinical, diagnostic, and therapeutic management of patients affected by adrenal disease, as well as to identify risk and/or predisposing factors for the development of the disease.

Study Design: Observational, longitudinal, single-center, non-interventional (without drug administration) study.

The study is divided into two phases:

FIRST PHASE (retrospective): registration of all patients affected by hypothalamic-pituitary-adrenal disease followed by the Adrenal Diseases Outpatient Clinic of the Endocrinology Unit at the AOU of Modena.

SECOND PHASE (prospective): enrollment of all patients affected by adrenal disease consecutively presenting to the Adrenal Diseases Outpatient Clinic of the Endocrinology Unit at the AOU of Modena.

Study Population Inclusion criteria: subjects affected by adrenal disease presenting to the Adrenal Diseases Outpatient Clinic of the Endocrinology Unit at the AOU of Modena, who are able to autonomously provide written informed consent.

Exclusion criteria: subjects under 18 years of age.

Study Methodologies An anonymized database will be created to collect data from patients presenting to the aforementioned outpatient clinic. Specifically, the data collected for each patient will include: demographic data, data related to the adrenal disease, symptoms, physical examination, radiological imaging, surgical intervention data, histological examination data, bio-humoral tests, hormonal tests, DEXA data, current replacement therapies data, current anti-secretory medical therapies data, data on other current pharmacological therapies, and comorbidities data.

brief_summary:
Bed bathing is a routine nursing procedure in the intensive care unit (ICU). In the study units, every patient routinely receives both a traditional bed bath with warm water and soap (every 10 days) and a bath with pre-packaged, disposable, no-rinse wipes (every 3 days). Little is known about how these two methods compare for pain, comfort and physiological stress in the same patient.

The goal of this randomized crossover trial is to compare the two bathing methods within the same adult ICU patients. The main question it aims to answer is: Does pain-related behavior during the bath, measured with the Critical-Care Pain Observation Tool (CPOT) while the patient is turned to the side, differ between the soap-and-water bath and the wipe bath? Other questions include whether the methods differ in vital signs and body temperature after the bath, anxiety, comfort, feeling of cleanliness, satisfaction and preference in patients who can self-report, bath duration, nursing time, cost, and adverse events.

The routine bathing schedule does not change. Only the order of each participant's first two study baths is decided by chance: either soap-and-water first and wipes 72 hours later, or wipes first and soap-and-water 72 hours later. Each patient serves as his or her own control. The first minute of the first lateral turn in both baths is video-recorded (face, upper body and arms only) and scored by an assessor who does not know which method was used.
primary_outcomes: Procedural pain behavior during the first lateral turn (CPOT)
title: Soap-and-Water Bed Bath Versus Disposable Wipe Bath in the Same ICU Patients

brief_summary:
Background:

Liver cirrhosis with ascites is a major health problem, and large-volume paracentesis (LVP) is commonly performed for management of tense or refractory ascites. However, LVP is associated with paracentesis-induced circulatory dysfunction (PICD), which can lead to renal impairment, hyponatremia, rapid recurrence of ascites, and increased mortality. Human albumin is the most effective plasma expander for prevention of PICD, but its high cost limits its use in resource-limited settings like Bangladesh.

Objective:

To compare the effectiveness of low-dose albumin (4 g/L) versus standard-dose albumin (6 g/L) in preventing PICD following large-volume paracentesis in patients with liver cirrhosis.

Methods:

This prospective randomized controlled clinical trial will be conducted in the Department of Hepatology, Bangladesh Medical University (BMU). Adult cirrhotic patients with tense or refractory ascites requiring LVP will be enrolled. Eligible participants will be randomly allocated into two groups: low-dose albumin (4 g/L) and standard-dose albumin (6 g/L). Baseline clinical and laboratory parameters, including plasma renin activity (PRA), will be recorded on day 0. After LVP, albumin will be administered according to group allocation. Patients will be followed up on Day 6 and Day 14 after LVP. Plasma renin activity will be reassessed on Day 6 for diagnosis of PICD, while renal and liver function tests will be reassessed on Day 14.. Data will be analyzed using SPSS, and p-value \<0.05 will be considered statistically significant.

Conclusion:

The study is expected to determine whether low-dose albumin is as effective as standard-dose albumin in preventing PICD. A positive result may support the use of a cost-effective regimen, improving accessibility and clinical outcomes in cirrhotic patients undergoing LVP.
primary_outcomes: Incidence of Paracentesis-Induced Circulatory Dysfunction (PICD) in patients of both groups,6th day following paracentesis
title: Low Dose Versus Standard Dose Albumin

brief_summary: This randomized clinical trial compares the effectiveness of a chlorhexidine mouthwash with an essential-oil-based mouthwash in improving oral health outcomes. Participants will be assigned to one of the two mouthwash groups and will use the assigned mouthwash according to the study protocol. Oral health parameters will be assessed at baseline and after the follow-up period to determine and compare the effects of the two mouthwashes.
primary_outcomes: The Orthodontic Plaque Index (OPI)
title: EFFECTIVENESS OF DILUTED CHLORHEXIDINE AND ESSENTIAL OIL BASED MOUTHWASHES ON PLAQUE IN ORTHODONTIC PATIENTS- A RANDOMIZED CONTROLLED TRIAL

brief_summary:
This study will investigate whether adding virtual reality-based optokinetic stimulation to neuromuscular training improves jump-landing movements, balance, and performance during a visually cued movement task in basketball players. Optokinetic stimulation involves watching moving visual patterns through a virtual reality headset. Neuromuscular training includes strength, balance, and jumping and landing exercises.

Forty-two licensed basketball players aged 16-35 years will be randomly assigned to one of three groups: usual team training alone (control group), neuromuscular training in addition to usual team training, or virtual reality-based optokinetic stimulation followed by neuromuscular training in addition to usual team training. The additional training will be provided three times per week for six weeks.

Assessments will be performed before and after the six-week program. The main outcome will be the maximum amount of knee bending during landing. Other assessments will examine landing forces, lower-limb movements, body movement, standing balance, and reliance on vision for balance. At the end of the program, participants will also complete a jump-landing task in response to colored lights to assess whether movement strategies are maintained under additional cognitive demands.
primary_outcomes: Change in Peak Knee Flexion Angle During Drop Vertical Jump Landing
title: Effects of Virtual Reality-Based Optokinetic Stimulation Added to Neuromuscular Training in Basketball Players

brief_summary:
Nerandomilast is an oral medicine that slows down the loss of functional residual capacity (FVC) in people with idiopathic pulmonary fibrosis (IPF) and progressive pulmonary fibrosis (PPF). It was tested in two large clinical trials in which participants were carefully selected. In everyday practice, patients are often older, have more other illnesses, or take additional medicines, and it is not known whether the benefits seen in the trials also occur outside them.

The Real-world Study of Nerandomilast (ReaSoN-IPF/PPF) follows people with IPF or PPF who begin nerandomilast as part of their usual medical care at several medical centers in Israel. The study does not assign any treatment; the treating physician makes every decision about therapy.

The main goal is to find out whether lung function declines more slowly once nerandomilast is started. Because patients have breathing tests before they begin the medicine as well as during treatment, each patient is compared with themselves: the rate at which their FVC was declining beforehand is compared with the rate following treatment.

The study also asks how patients feel, using a questionnaire called the K-BILD, and records side effects, hospital admissions, disease exacerbations, and whether patients stop the medicine.

Participants attend their normal clinic visits. They complete the questionnaire before treatment starts and again at 6 to 12 months, and their routine lung function results are collected. No extra tests or visits are required beyond the questionnaire.
primary_outcomes: Adverse events
title: Real-world Study of Nerandomilast in Patients With Idiopathic Pulmonary Fibrosis and Progressive Pulmonary Fibrosis

brief_summary: This study examined the relationship between engagement-based academic advising and undergraduate nursing students' academic success, focusing on term-to-term retention, annual credit completion, and cumulative grade point average (GPA). It also investigated whether advisor active-empathic listening mediated these relationships and whether the associations differed according to first-generation status and scholarship eligibility. A prospective cluster-randomized mixed-methods study was conducted among 995 first-year undergraduate nursing students assigned to 30 academic advisors. Data were collected using student-reported and observer-rated listening measures, institutional academic records, and qualitative information about advising implementation. Students with high exposure to engagement-based advising had higher odds of term-to-term retention, completed more annual credits, and achieved higher cumulative GPAs than students with low exposure. Advisor active-empathic listening partially mediated the associations between advising exposure and all three academic outcomes, accounting for approximately 40%-46% of the total effects. The association between advising exposure and GPA was stronger among first-generation students, whereas the interaction with scholarship eligibility was not statistically significant. These findings highlight the potential importance of proactive advising, collaborative academic planning, and attentive, responsive communication in supporting undergraduate persistence and achievement. The results may inform the development and evaluation of student-support strategies in nursing education, although further research across diverse institutions is needed to confirm generalizability and strengthen causal interpretation.
primary_outcomes: Term-to-Term Undergraduate Student Retention Rate
title: Active-Empathic Listening and Student Persistence

brief_summary: A pioneer periodontal surgical approach employing the closed surgical technique (CST) has been designed to gain access to isolated interdental periodontal defects and retain the soft-tissue architecture. This technique is based on a modified tunnelling technique to retract full-thickness gingival flaps from the osseous defect in a closed manner retaining intact the interproximal papilla thus, suturing is not required. A randomized controlled clinical trial will determine the efficacy of the CST combined with i-PRF versus the modified papilla preservation technique (MPPT) combined with i-PRF over a period of 12 months

Cementoenamel junction to Bottom of the defect
title: A Closed Surgical Technique vs Modified Papilla Preservation Technique

brief_summary:
Bariatric surgery can help people achieve significant weight loss and improve obesity-related health conditions. However, maintaining these benefits requires long-term adherence to recommended lifestyle changes, including healthy eating habits, regular physical activity, taking prescribed vitamin and mineral supplements, following medication recommendations, and attending scheduled postoperative appointments.

Some patients experience difficulties following these recommendations during the first months after surgery, which may affect their recovery and long-term health outcomes.

The purpose of this study is to evaluate whether an early postoperative, nurse-led, individualized counseling program can improve adherence to lifestyle recommendations among adults who have undergone bariatric surgery.

Participants will be randomly assigned to one of two groups. The intervention group will receive an individualized counseling program delivered by a trained nurse, in addition to routine postoperative care. The program will focus on identifying individual barriers to lifestyle adherence, providing tailored education and counseling, setting realistic goals, developing personalized action plans, and reinforcing recommended self-management behaviors. The control group will receive routine postoperative care.

The study will assess participants' adherence to recommended postoperative lifestyle behaviors, including dietary recommendations, physical activity, vitamin and mineral supplementation, medication use, and attendance at scheduled follow-up appointments.

It is hypothesized that participants receiving the individualized nurse-led counseling program will demonstrate better adherence to postoperative lifestyle recommendations than those receiving routine care alone.

The findings may help identify an effective nursing approach to supporting patients during early recovery after bariatric surgery and maintaining recommended lifestyle changes.
interventions: Early Postoperative Nurse-Led Individualized Lifestyle Counseling Program
primary_outcomes: Change in Dietary Adherence Score from Baseline to Follow-Up
title: Effectiveness of an Early Postoperative Nurse-Led, Individualized Counseling Program on Lifestyle Adherence After Bariatric Surgery: A Randomized Controlled Trial
